analysis.one_liner: Bans road-building and most logging in undeveloped national forest land, with limited exceptions.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it sat in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee from May 2007 until the Congress ended in January 2009, despite 20 senators signing on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made permanent, by law, the ban on building new roads in inventoried roadless areas of the National Forest System — the large undeveloped chunks of national forest. It also banned cutting or removing timber in those areas, with narrow exceptions for safety emergencies, habitat restoration, and existing mineral leases. The bill's stated purpose was to protect drinking water sources, fish and wildlife habitat, and recreation land.
analysis.who_benefits: People who get drinking water from the more than 354 municipal watersheds located in roadless areas, and anyone who hikes, camps, hunts, or fishes in national forests. The bill argued that keeping these areas unroaded saves downstream communities millions in water filtration costs and preserves habitat for imperiled species.

how_it_helps.text: Bars road construction and reconstruction in inventoried roadless areas, with exceptions only for imminent threats to life or property, environmental cleanup, safety projects, federal-aid highways, and leases already in effect on January 12, 2001.
Prohibits cutting, selling, or removing timber in roadless areas, except for infrequent, small-diameter cuts aimed at habitat improvement or reducing wildfire risk.

The bill's findings state that roadless areas supply drinking water to millions of citizens through 354 municipal watersheds and save downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs.
The bill's findings state roadless areas provide settings for hiking, camping, hunting, fishing, skiing, and similar activities, and protect habitat for threatened and endangered species.
The bill's findings state the impact on the timber supply would be less than 0.5 percent nationally, and the National Forest System supplies only about 0.4 percent of U.S. oil and gas production.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and oil, gas, and mining operators with interests in roadless national forest areas, plus rural communities that depend on timber jobs. The bill argues the national impact is small — under 0.5 percent of timber supply — but the losses would be concentrated in specific forests and towns.

drawbacks.text: Logging and mining access to roadless areas would be curtailed, and the economic losses would fall on a small number of rural, timber-dependent communities even if the national timber impact is under half a percent, as the bill itself states.

The prohibitions would be permanent by design: the bill says they cannot be reconsidered, modified, or terminated through the normal forest planning process, locking in the policy without flexibility if conditions change.

Opponents have long argued that limited road access is needed for firefighting and forest management; the bill counters with its own finding that fires are almost twice as likely in roaded areas, but the tradeoff between access and protection is a genuine management dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protected broadly shared public goods — clean drinking water, wildlife habitat, and recreation land — at a cost the bill's own analysis puts at less than 0.5 percent of national timber supply and a fraction of an already small federal share of oil and gas production. The real cost is local and real: towns built around national forest timber work would bear losses the bill does not compensate. The permanent, inflexible nature of the prohibition is a fair criticism, though it was the point — supporters wanted protection that a future administration could not undo administratively.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on May 24, 2007, with 19 cosponsors: 17 Democrats, 1 Republican (John Warner of Virginia), and 1 Independent.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 110th Congress in January 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, oil, gas, and mining interests kept access to roadless national forest land. The public got no statutory protection for drinking water sources and recreation areas, and supporters had to start over in the next Congress.

for.name: 17 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Bingaman, Boxer, Clinton, Obama, Kerry, Durbin, and Feinstein.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to; never acted
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — from referral in May 2007 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Timber and extractive industries
against.what_they_did: Opposed national roadless-area protections, which would have restricted logging, drilling, and mining access on tens of millions of acres of national forest.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 20 sponsors and cosponsors, 18 were Democrats or Independents and one was a Republican (John Warner); the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.note: The bill bans cutting, selling, or removing timber in inventoried roadless areas, except for limited habitat and wildfire-risk work. The bill's own findings put the national timber supply impact under 0.5 percent, but the losses would concentrate in specific forests and timber-dependent towns.

New road construction for mineral development is barred except to service leases already in effect on January 12, 2001. The bill's findings note national forests supply only about 0.4 percent of U.S. oil and gas, with roadless areas a fraction of that.
The bill preserves unroaded settings for hiking, camping, hunting, fishing, and similar activities, which depend on undeveloped land staying that way.

industries.industry: Municipal water systems and downstream communities
industries.note: The bill's findings say roadless areas provide drinking water through 354 municipal watersheds and save downstream communities millions in filtration costs by keeping watersheds undisturbed.
